power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Affective science is the interdisciplinary study of phenomena such as emotions, moods, attitudes, and stress responses, which together make up a large part of the forces that energize and direct behavior.
The field has developed rich theories of motivation and emotion and generated an impressively large empirical literature on affect in human and nonhuman behavior.
In this paper, I argue that the field is now well poised for a systematic turn toward computational modeling.
I begin by explaining what computational modeling is, trace how it has transformed neighboring disciplines, and lay out what affective science stands to gain from it.
Many computational models of affect and motivation already exist, but this work remains scattered across fields that rarely speak to one another.

I review this work across three interrelated domains: (1) models of specific, circumscribed affective phenomena; (2) applied models in computational psychiatry and affective computing; and (3) broader theoretical models that aim to explain what affect is and how it arises.

Finally, I outline a vision for the new field of Computational Affective Science-one that transcends the boundary between affect and cognition in pursuit of a cumulative science of motivated behavior.

Introduction "Feelings come and go like clouds in a windy sky. " -Thích Nhất Hạnh, 1997 From the earliest civilizations, human beings have cast anxious eyes towards clouds in the windy sky, captivated by forces that seemed powerful, consequential, and often beyond their control.

text.text: Some of these forces, like storms and droughts, were external.
Others, like grief, fear, or love-internal.
Across centuries and cultures, both have inspired superstitions, careful observations, and, eventually, scientific explanations.
Ancient peoples relied on omens and rituals to placate the destructive powers behind floods and droughts.
Babylonian scribes recorded rudimentary correlations between thunder and rain-patterns so obvious to us now that we forget that such connections had to be discovered in the first place.

In Ancient Greece, Aristotle's work outlining the water cycle allowed early meteorologists to use cues such as cloud shapes and wind directions to make the first reliable predictions about the weather.
Over the centuries that followed, meteorology matured into one of the great success stories of modern science, able to track hurricanes from space and predict storms days in advance.
Emotions, much like storms and sunshine, have been viewed throughout human history as powerful and often unpredictable forces that can have a profound impact on our lives.
Ancient peoples believed that those in the throes of mental torment were being punished by gods.
Galen and his contemporaries began searching for regularities and underlying mechanisms, proposing that different moods reflected changes in the balance of bodily "humors."
Later thinkers, such as Descartes and Darwin, sought to categorize emotions and identify the principles governing their expression.

Fortunately, the story of meteorology is not an isolated one (see Winsberg, 2010).

text.text: In fact, the behavioral sciences have their own version of this story.

In the mid-20th century, the cognitive revolution transformed the field still shrouded by the long shadow of behaviorism by insisting that unobservable mental processes could-and should-be specified in formal mathematical terms (Bruner et al., 1956 (Bruner et al., /2017)).

Affect had already been kept at arm's length from mainstream psychology during the behaviorist era.

text.text: What remains missing is a systematic synthesis of these efforts with one another and with the rich theoretical traditions of affective science-a synthesis that would expand the methodological toolkit of affective science and open the door to new kinds of questions for cognitive science, in pursuit of a truly cumulative science of behavior.
In the sections that follow, I offer a definition of computational modeling as it applies to the study of affect and outline why this approach matters by working through concrete examples.

I then proceed to survey the emerging landscape of Computational Affective Science, highlighting the transformative opportunities that it holds for uniting theoretical rigor with formal precision in the study of the forces that make us tick.
Before going further, it is worth pausing to clarify what I mean by computational modeling.
I expect readers will come to this discussion from different starting points: some already fluent in computational modeling, many others engaging deeply with it for the first time.
Complicating matters further, the term itself has carried different meanings across history and disciplines.
A shared working definition is, therefore, in order.
Broadly, computational models in the behavioral sciences serve one of two aims.
Explanatory models translate theories and hypotheses about how a phenomenon arises into precise equations and algorithms, with the goal of making those theories explicit enough to simulate and test.

Predictive models, including many COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE machine-learning approaches, are optimized to forecast an outcome without making strong claims about the process that generated it (Shmueli, 2010).
text.formatted: Predictive models, including many COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE machine-learning approaches, are optimized to forecast an outcome without making strong claims about the process that generated it <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Shmueli, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: These two aims are often complementary, since predictive models can surface new regularities that explanatory models must account for.

Accordingly, throughout this paper, I use the term computational modeling in a deliberately capacious sense, to refer to any approach that translates ideas about affect from words into equations or algorithms in a way that advances our understanding of how affective processes arise and how they shape behavior and cognition.
Importantly, computational modeling is not a single method.
Instead, it is useful to think of computational modeling as a spectrum defined by the tightness of the link between the psychological hypothesis and the mathematical form it takes.

A model can take the form of a Bayesian model, a reinforcement learning algorithm, a neural network, or something else entirely, as long as it faithfully expresses the modeler's hypothesis about the phenomenon under study.

The tightness of the link between the description of a hypothesized process and its mathematical formulation is what distinguishes a computational model from a statistical model (Guest & Martin, 2021).
text.formatted: The tightness of the link between the description of a hypothesized process and its mathematical formulation is what distinguishes a computational model from a statistical model <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Guest & Martin, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A researcher can fit a linear regression to a dataset to test whether two variables are related, without claiming that the structure of the equation mirrors the process that generated the data.

But the same linear regression equation can be considered a computational model if the substantive hypothesis is that increases in quantity x drive changes in quantity y, and that this effect is constant across the range of x.
Imagine, for example, walking into a local bakery and trying to figure out why different cookie boxes have different price tags.

If you suspect that the price of a box of cookies is simply the price of a single cookie multiplied by the number of cookies in a box, then you may formalize your hypothesis as a linear regression and test your model by comparing its predictions against real data.
In many cases, hypotheses in psychology are richer than that.

For example, we might hypothesize that the reason why a person who has just moved into the neighborhood buys a different cookie on each visit to a bakery during their first month, before eventually settling on double chocolate chunk every time, is that they are gradually updating their beliefs about the value of each option until they can identify a favorite.

In this case, a Bayesian belief-updating model (i.e., a model in which a person starts with initial beliefs about how good each option is and revises them in a principled way after every new experience) does a much better job of capturing the hypothesized process, though a linear regression of variability in cookie choice over time may still serve as a useful description of the data.
Finally, it is worth making explicit what building a computational model involves in practice, since the rest of this paper returns to these steps repeatedly.
A model typically has four ingredients.
The first is a set of variables: the quantities the model takes in and produces, such as the stimuli it sees and the choices or ratings it makes.
The second is a set of rules (i.e., equations or an algorithm) that specify how inputs are transformed into outputs and that embody the hypothesis itself.
The third is a set of parameters: adjustable quantities within those rules, such as a learning rate (how much a single experience changes one's expectations).

The fourth ingredient is a way of evaluating the model: researchers simulate it to see what behavior it predicts, fit it to real data to estimate its parameters, and compare it against competing models that embody alternative hypotheses, asking which one best accounts for the data without unnecessary complexity.
Together, these distinctions offer a lens for the rest of this paper.

For any model discussed, it is worth asking whether its primary aim is to explain or to predict, how tightly its COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE mathematical form is tied to a psychological hypothesis, and what its variables, rules, parameters, and evaluations reveal about the phenomenon under study.

At its core, computational modeling is the practice of translating psychological hypotheses from whatever language we already use to guide experimental exploration and write papers into the language of math.
Of course, anyone who has tried to carry out even a casual conversation in a second language-much less do rigorous science in it-knows how demanding such translation can be.
Why, then, invest all this time and effort into learning another language when affective science already makes steady progress?

It is true that affective science has made remarkable progress in turning rich everyday phenomena into objects of scientific study and providing useful explanations for how they arise and influence behavior.

However, as things currently stand, most such explanations exist at the level of verbal theories-empirically-grounded accounts, stated in natural language, of why people feel what they feel, and what roles those feelings play in everything from memory and decision-making to physical health and mental well-being.
Over the years, these theories have guided measurement choices, motivated innovative experimental paradigms, and directly informed clinical interventions.
They rest on a large body of rigorous experimental evidence.
Yet an important limitation remains, and, with it, an important opportunity.
Natural language is rich, expressive, and relatable, but it is also imprecise.
When the goal at stake is to articulate the exact mechanisms and generate quantitative, falsifiable predictions about affective phenomena, it often falls short.
To see why, let us consider research on anxiety as a case study both in how far the field has come and why computational affective science marks the next frontier.
Vivid descriptions of anxiety-a familiar and sometimes debilitating cacophony of dread, worry, a racing heart, and a menacing pit in one's stomach-date back at least two and a half millennia.
Anxiety is a normal and often helpful emotion, but it can also become a clinical concern when it is excessive and debilitating, as in the case of anxiety disorders.
Ancient Greek and Roman texts attributed anxiety-like states to the weight of confronting one's own mortality (Crocq, 2015).

text.text: Modern scientific accounts characterize anxiety as being rooted in a more general overestimation of threat (Abramowitz & Blakey, 2020).

text.text: This perspective is supported by an extensive body of empirical work showing that anxiety makes people more likely to interpret ambiguous cues as threatening (Neta et al., 2017; G. Park et al., 2016); is associated with the tendency to overestimate the duration, severity, and probability of threatening events (Dev et al., 2023; Jusyte et al., 2015; Muris & Van Der Heiden, 2006); and predicts better recall of threatrelated information (Herrera et al., 2017).

Park et al., 2016)</ref>; is associated with the tendency to overestimate the duration, severity, and probability of threatening events <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Dev et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Jusyte et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Muris & Van Der Heiden, 2006)</ref>; and predicts better recall of threatrelated information <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Herrera et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, this evidence makes "overestimation of threat" a compelling and actionable framework for both understanding anxiety as an emotion and treating anxiety disorders.
But what exactly counts as "overestimation"?
This is precisely the kind of question where a verbal theory lets us leave important choices unstated.
Consider three distinct mechanisms, each of which could plausibly produce what we observe and describe as "overestimation of threat."
The first possibility is that anxiety shifts one's starting assumptions-or prior beliefs-about danger, so that an anxious person walks into a novel social situation already expecting it to go poorly.
Before anyone has said anything, they may assume others will judge them negatively, that they will say something awkward, or that the interaction will be uncomfortable.
The second possibility is that anxiety changes how people interpret uncertainty.

In this case, a person does not necessarily assume that the situation is dangerous from the outset, but COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE when something is unclear or ambiguous, they are quicker to treat it as a potential threat.
Someone laughs after they speak-are they laughing with them or at them?
By lowering the threshold for treating ambiguous cues as threatening, anxiety pushes the interpretation toward the latter option.
Finally, the third possibility is that anxiety slows down learning.

Here, the issue is not the initial assumption or the interpretation of ambiguity, but the updating process: even when the environment turns out to be safe, it takes longer for an anxious person to internalize that safety.
A conversation may go well, others may respond positively, and nothing bad happens-but this single experience has little impact.
It takes many repeated positive interactions before the person begins to expect that things will go well.
Each interpretation is plausible.
Each is consistent with existing findings.
And yet, each yields different quantitative predictions and warrants different experiments for testing those predictions.
Crucially, in the case of anxiety disorders, different mechanisms of threatoverestimation necessitate different levers for clinical intervention.

In closing this section, I want to acknowledge that some behavioral and affective scientists reading this might have a visceral reaction to the suggestion of reducing the richness of human affect to a set of equations-an understandable concern, especially for those of us who have witnessed the depth of emotional suffering like the torment of an anxiety disorder or the paralysis of grief firsthand.
But one thing needs to be made clear: the goal of computational modeling is not to replace that complexity.
In fact, the aim is to capture it, which makes observation and empirical insight indispensable.
Rich observational data give us the patterns, intuitions, and phenomenological richness that models seek to formalize in the first place.
What computational modeling offers is a way to take those insights and render them precise enough to fail.

Understood this way, computational modeling is not so much an assortment of techniques as it is an integrated philosophical and methodological approach that can complement existing practices in the field.

The anxiety example illustrates one of the central strengths of computational modeling: its ability to transform broad verbal explanations into explicit mechanistic accounts that can be tested against one another.
But this is only one part of a much larger story.

The same kinds of advances that reshaped research on memory, perception, language, and decision-making point to a broader set of advantages that computational modeling can bring to the study of affect.
Let me highlight three interrelated advantages that deserve particular emphasis.
A compelling example of this affordance of computational modeling comes from one of the earliest attempts at formal theorizing in psychology.

For many years, the dominant account of perception postulated that a signal-such as a quiet sound or a quickly presented image-either crossed a fixed sensory threshold or did not, rendering detection of said signal all-or-none.

An alternative hypothesis put forth by Swets et al. (1961) proposed that every observation was instead a reflection of overlapping distributions of both signal and noise, with an observer playing the role of a decision-maker who is actively setting a criterion for determining whether a signal was present or not.
text.formatted: An alternative hypothesis put forth by <ref type="bibr" target="#b162">Swets et al. (1961)</ref> proposed that every observation was instead a reflection of overlapping distributions of both signal and noise, with an observer playing the role of a decision-maker who is actively setting a criterion for determining whether a signal was present or not.

text.text: Notice that the two hypotheses give rise to the same qualitative prediction: people are more likely to detect strong signals and less likely to detect weak ones.

However, once formalized, signal detection theory predicted that, as the criterion shifts from more liberal to more conservative, the resulting combinations of hit and false alarm rates should fall along a characteristic nonlinear receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, even as one's sensitivity to the stimulus (d') remains unchanged.
Empirical data from studies that force participants to adopt deliberately strict or loose criteria (e.g., by incentivizing accuracy vs. speed) consistently matched this pattern.
By cleanly separating what an observer can sense from how they choose to respond, this work paved the way for the study of perception, memory, and decision-making as we know them today.

text.text: Crucially, this formalization generated a series of non-obvious predictions.
First, the prediction that once a cue is reliably paired with the reward, the timing of the dopamine spike should shift from the presentation of the reward itself to the cue that predicts it.
And second, that if an expected reward then fails to materialize, dopamine activity should dip below baseline.

Notice that questions about the precise timing of a neural response, or about whether an effect grows linearly or nonlinearly over time, rarely arise from verbal theorizing because they seem too narrow to matter.
Yet it is precisely such specific, non-obvious predictions that provide the strongest support for a proposed mechanism.
Like a spotlight illuminating a previously neglected corner of the conceptual terrain, this model inspired researchers to measure dopamine activity at moments that previously seemed unimportant.
Recordings from midbrain dopamine neurons revealed exactly the predicted pattern of activity (Schultz et al., 1997).

text.text: This is just one example of how an entirely new understanding-one that is now largely taken for granted-COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE emerged in large part because efforts at creating computational models generated new, testable hypotheses about what those hidden dynamics might be.
How many similarly rich hypotheses about affect remain dormant today, waiting for computational models to bring them to light?
Only sustained investment in computational approaches in affective science will tell.
Formal models can let us explore scenarios that are effectively off-limits because of cost, duration, impossibility of experimental manipulation, or ethical constraints.
We could never (thankfully!) systematically expose children to chronic stress to study its emotional toll.
We can, however, examine related mechanisms "in silico."
Many examples of this strategy emerged from the connectionist tradition, where researchers used artificial neural networks to probe mechanisms spanning multiple levels of analysis.
For example, in order to study the etiology of acquired dyslexia experimentally, one would, in principle, need to lesion the brain regions that are believed to support reading.
Instead, researchers trained neural networks to map spelling onto meaning and then "lesioned" the model directly by selectively removing connections after learning had taken place.
The lesioned models reproduced the hallmark errors of deep dyslexia, including semantic confusions such as reading "cat" as "dog" (Hinton & Shallice, 1991; Plaut & Shallice, 1993).

text.text: Taken together, these examples demonstrate how systematically applying computational tools can help adjudicate between competing accounts, surface surprising predictions, and probe questions that remain off-limits to empirical research.
The remainder of this paper asks what the same turn to computational modeling might look like for affective science.
At present, there is no single, coherent field that calls itself "Computational Affective Science."
Nevertheless, attempts to formalize affective processes have been growing across psychology, cognitive science, neuroscience, psychiatry, and other disciplines.
These efforts often proceed in isolation, using different terminology, publishing in different venues, and rarely speaking to one another despite frequently trying to solve the same problems.

Recognizing these efforts as part of a shared enterprise would make it easier for ideas, methods, and findings to accumulate across traditional disciplinary boundaries and help build toward a more unified understanding of affect and motivation and, ultimately, intelligent behavior more broadly.
I synthesize the existing computational work on affect into three interconnected domains organized by their goals.
First, models of specific phenomena seek to isolate and formalize circumscribed processes like emotion regulation or social emotion inference.

Second, applied models are built to accomplish real-world goals that extend beyond scientific understanding, whether by detecting and measuring affect, intervening on it, or generating it in artificial systems (as in computational psychiatry and affective computing).

Third, theoretical models attempt to synthesize across phenomena and applications in order to answer fundamental questions about the nature of affect and its role within the broader architecture of the mind.
Together, these COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE domains reveal the contours of an emerging field that I refer to as Computational Affective Science (Figure 1).

text.text: A framework for computational affective science.
The three domains are positioned by their aim (explanation vs. application) and scope (narrow vs. broad).

Models of specific phenomena (e.g., emotion regulation, social affective cognition) formalize circumscribed processes; applied models (computational psychiatry, affective computing) use formal models to achieve practical goals; and theoretical models integrate across phenomena and levels of analysis to formalize broad theories of affect and motivation.
Great science often begins with a simple observation.
We notice, for example, that people feel regret in the face of a missed opportunity.
Observations like these serve as the foundation for our hypotheses.
We hypothesize that missed opportunities lead to regret, and we create experimental settings-that either involve missed opportunities or not-to test our intuitions.
But we rarely stop there.

We might further hypothesize, for example, that it is not the missed opportunities per se that cause regret, but a particular type of appraisal: one that involves a counterfactual comparison between what happened and what could have happened (van Dijk & Zeelenberg, 2002).

text.text: Notice that the second hypothesis is much harder to test.

To establish the causal role of counterfactual appraisals in the experience of regret, the ideal experiment would randomly assign people to either think counterfactually or not while keeping the situation constant.

Yet we cannot reach into a participant's brain and turn their "appraisal knobs" up or down, and we know that simply instructing people not to think counterfactually would be about as effective as instructing them not to think about a white bear (see Wegner & Schneider, 2003).

text.text: We can, of course, instruct some participants to think counterfactually and compare them with participants who receive no such instruction.
Such designs do support causal inference, but they are imperfect, since the instruction offers only coarse control over how strongly the appraisal is engaged.

Similarly, asking people to recall whether they appraised a situation in a certain way, or to explain why they chose one emotion regulation strategy over another, can yield biased or confabulated responses, particularly when people are asked about the causes of a specific reaction (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977; see also Ericsson & Simon, 1980).

Computational modeling offers a complementary path forward.
Just as meteorologists build artificial tornadoes and dial the artificial humidity knobs, we can build artificial participants and directly manipulate their appraisals, beliefs, goals, and much more.

The models reviewed here begin to bridge traditionally separate domains-emotion perception, theory of mind, social learning, and interpersonal emotion regulation-within a common computational language centered on dynamic belief updating and action selection.
Emotion Regulation.
How do people choose which emotion regulation strategies to use at any given moment?

In one example of a recently developed model, Petter et al. (2025) aimed COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE to offer a mechanistic explanation for the robust effect of emotional intensity on regulatory strategy choice: the finding that people tend to favor reappraisal (an emotion regulation strategy that involves changing one's interpretation of the situation in order to change its emotional impact, McRae et al., 2012) at low stimulus intensities and distraction at high intensities (Matthews et al., 2021; Sheppes et al., 2011).

text.text: In contrast, distraction is stimulus-independent and should take more-or-less the same amount of time to implement regardless of the stimulus.
The emerging hypothesis, then, is that opting for distraction leads to less overall time spent in a highly negative emotional state, making it a more desirable option in high-intensity situations.

Model simulations show that when this cost-benefit trade-off is built into the decisionmaking process of simulated participants, they spontaneously replicate the empirical pattern, preferring reappraisal at low intensities and distraction at high (Petter et al., 2025).

text.text: Instead of being hard-coded into the model, the preference for distraction at high intensity emerges from the hypothesized trade-off between how long each strategy takes to work and how much time is then spent in a highly negative state.

Because the model makes these assumptions explicit, alternative accounts (e.g., that distraction is preferred at high intensity simply because it is less cognitively demanding) can be formalized and compared against it on the same footing.
Importantly, this is not a result the model produces in a vacuum: it depends on decades of empirical work.

Building on that foundation, the model yields a concrete mechanistic hypothesis that can be tested empirically by manipulating the time available to regulate-an experimental design that would be difficult to motivate without the structure that the model provides.

Extending the horizon from isolated instances of emotion regulation to lifelong learning, other models simulate how virtual agents learn which emotion regulation strategies are most effective in a given environment, depending on past outcomes and stable personality traits (Abro et al., 2015; Bosse et al., 2010).

text.text: By instantiating the regulation process in a simulated environment with changing affective demands, these models provide insight into how agents balance short-and long-term benefits of different strategies.

These models, too, yield concrete and testable predictions-such as which trait profiles should gravitate toward distraction in unpredictable environments, or how strategy repertoires should change with feedback-that can be evaluated in laboratory tasks and longitudinal designs.

Each model reviewed here formalizes the same core architecture: an agent in a dynamic environment, who has access to a limited repertoire of regulatory strategies; incurs costs for deploying those strategies; and must balance immediate emotional relief against longer-term stability and adaptation.

This shared architecture, along with the shared formal language that speaks of value, dynamics, and learning, puts these models on a common footing, allowing insights to accumulate across models and levels of analyses.
The work reviewed so far seeks to understand affective phenomena for their own sake.

Applied models are defined by aims that extend beyond scientific understanding: they are built to accomplish goals in the real world, whether by detecting and measuring affect, intervening on it, or engineering systems that produce affective behavior of their own.

Two areas are especially relevant to the emerging field of computational affective science: computational psychiatry, COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE which formalizes affective dysfunction in order to predict and treat it, and affective computing, which builds emotion-aware algorithms and agents.

Unlike the models reviewed in the previous section, which focused on explaining specific affective phenomena, the work reviewed here is organized around broader domains that use computational models to not only understand the affective mind but to achieve practical goals.
Affect dysregulation lies at the heart of many psychiatric conditions, from depression and anxiety to schizophrenia and personality disorders (Aldao et al., 2010; Beck, 1971; Gross & Jazaieri, 2014).

text.text: The emerging field of computational psychiatrywhich aims to formalize the mechanisms underlying mental illness-offers a particularly rich and relevant context for computational affective science.
The goal of computational psychiatry is not only to understand affect, but to clarify its dysfunction, predict symptom trajectories, and, ultimately, improve treatment outcomes.

Individual papers in this literature also vary in how close they are to the clinic, with some offering primarily theoretical accounts of a disorder and others developing tools for treatment selection.
Given the breadth of this literature, what follows is a selective review highlighting advances that are most relevant for computational affective scientists.
One prominent area of work models specific symptoms that manifest as breakdowns in emotion generation or regulation processes.

For example, reinforcement learning (RL) has been widely applied to characterize the mechanisms behind rumination (Bedder et al., 2024), dysregulation of effort-reward trade-offs in depression (Berwian et al., 2020), and anhedonia (Chase et al., 2010).

For affective scientists, this work offers not only methodological tools but a reminder that understanding emotion in full requires engaging with its dysfunction; and just as computational psychiatry stands to benefit from basic affective science, affective science may find some of its most urgent applications in the clinic.
From affective robots, to emotion-detection software, to mentalhealth chatbots, affective computing has blossomed in recent years.

Its primary goal has historically focused on the development of useful applications; engineering systems that can themselves recognize and express emotion, and, ultimately, engage in motivated behavior (Picard, 1997).

text.text: A common belief in engineering, bringing us back to Richard Feynman, is that truly understanding something means being able to build it.
In practice, though, the arrow points in both directions, with deeper understanding emerging as a by-product of trying to make a system work.
In this section, I highlight several ways affective computing has begun to generate such understanding.
Emotion detection from facial expressions, natural language, and physiology has long been of interest to engineers and researchers in the field of affective computing.

Many of the models in this space are so-called performance-driven models, that is, models with no expectation of interpretability but instead designed with the goal of optimizing performance (e.g., D'Mello et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2020; Martínez & Yannakakis, 2010; Shukla et al., 2017).

Yet, because research in affective computing is largely driven by incentives to optimize performance, many of these models have not been explicitly pitted against one another to evaluate their theoretical commitments.
This leaves a wealth of theoretical insights unexplored.
Luckily, this is precisely the kind of opportunity that the emerging field of computational affective science will be well positioned to seize.

text.text: Beyond their practical utility, affective agents can also serve as "model organisms" for affective scientists.

Even if the internal mechanisms by which these agents generate affective outputs are not isomorphic to those of biological agents (i.e., the tightness of the link between the hypothesized process and the algorithmic form it takes is low), they can still serve as useful tools for basic science.

This logic is familiar from other areas of computational science: artificial neural networks are not literal models of the brain, yet, as we saw earlier, lesioning them has yielded important insights into neuropsychological phenomena.

Similarly, language models likely do not reason like humans do, yet recent years have seen a surge of work treating large language models (LLMs) as proxies for exploring a myriad of cognitive and linguistic phenomena (e.g., Binz & Schulz, 2023; Kosinski, 2024; McCoy et al., 2024; Prystawski et al., 2023; Ullman, 2023).

text.text: The same logic can be extended to the study of affect and motivation: we can manipulate the "wiring" of artificial agents and compare their behavior to human data.

Discrepancies can point to mis-specified mechanisms in the artificial models or to unexamined assumptions in existing theories, inspiring new hypotheses amenable to novel empirical and computational work.

In closing this section, even a cursory overview of models in affective computing makes it clear that there is a growing need for more cross-talk among engineers, computer scientists, and affective scientists.
Application-oriented models can almost certainly be improved with theoretical input and lessons from decades of empirical work.

Likewise, affective scientists can benefit from leveraging existing applications as in-silico laboratories-probing their errors, stress-testing their generalization, and drawing inspiration for new formal frameworks.
Embracing computational affective science as a shared identity can catalyze such exchanges and propel us toward both richer theories of affect and more humane technologies.
The specific models and real-world applications surveyed in the preceding sections are the raw bricks of science, but bricks alone do not make a house.

The third and final domain of computational affective science is also its most ambitious: it seeks to move beyond isolated phenomena and applications toward comprehensive, formal theories of affect-and, in doing so, to sharpen our answers to the most fundamental questions the field has been asking all along.
Over time, scientists integrate countless isolated empirical observations (and, increasingly, formal models) into broader theories that aim to explain affective life writ large.
Verbal theories continue to do much of this heavy lifting in affective science.
They have generated decades of testable predictions, organized vast swaths of empirical findings, and offered rich accounts of why people do what they do and feel what they feel.
Translating these theories into explicit algorithms adds a layer of precision, sharpening the theories' predictions and placing competing accounts on equal footing.
What distinguishes theoretical work from the more targeted modeling reviewed above is the ambition of theoretical models to synthesize not only across phenomena, but across levels of analysis.

The theories discussed next live mostly at Marr's computational and algorithmic levels (Marr, 1982; see also Griffiths et al., 2015), which describe, respectively, what problem a system is solving and what procedure it uses to solve it.

Of the three broad domains in this review (Models of Specific Phenomena, Applied Models, and Theoretical Models), theoretical modeling has been the least cumulative.
The reason for this is not that the work that has been done is weaker, but that synthesizing across phenomena, disciplines, modeling approaches, and levels of analysis is genuinely hard.
What follows is, therefore, best viewed as a map of promising avenues.
One of the deepest questions in affective science concerns why we feel the way we feel.
Verbal theories have offered a range of possible answers that agree on many observations yet diverge on the mechanisms behind them.
More recently, computational work has begun to translate these answers into the language of equations and algorithms.

This point matters well beyond debates about the nature of emotion.

If affect emerges from, and feeds back into, the same processes that support perception, attention, memory, and decision-making, then cognitive scientists cannot fully model those processes while leaving affect out.
Taken together, these efforts show how formalization can sharpen theoretical debates and help uncover areas where seeming disagreements may arise from a difference in emphasis or level of analysis.
The following section takes up the question that these models leave largely unanswered: how are such computations realized at the neural level?
Implementational Level Models.

While computational affective science aims to formalize the mechanisms of motivation and emotion at the computational and algorithmic levels, computational affective neuroscience seeks to ground these mechanisms in the brain.
Its cross-level insights inform computational modeling in basic affective science, highlighting what is neurally plausible and which constructs are reflected in brain activity.

Perhaps the most valuable contribution of neuroscience to computational affective science, then, is constraint: testing whether the mechanisms posited at the computational and algorithmic levels can be implemented in the brain, and understanding how interacting brain systems give rise to affect.
The dominant approach in affective neuroscience has traditionally relied on brain mapping: identifying which brain regions respond to which emotional states or stimuli.
This work has been enormously productive in cataloguing where in the brain affective processes show their fingerprints.

At the same time, several scholars have argued that brain mapping, while a powerful tool for localization, is less well suited to characterizing how the affective phenomena we observe at the computational and algorithmic levels are implemented in the brain (Niv, 2021; Uttal, 2001; Wixted & Mickes, 2013).

text.text: A large part of computational modeling in affective neuroscience relies on powerful machine learning algorithms.

Machine learning, which entails training algorithms to detect statistical regularities in large datasets, has often been criticized as a black-box approach that can achieve high predictive accuracy yet offer little mechanistic insight (Rudin, 2019).
text.formatted: Machine learning, which entails training algorithms to detect statistical regularities in large datasets, has often been criticized as a black-box approach that can achieve high predictive accuracy yet offer little mechanistic insight <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Rudin, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Yet recent advances in computational affective neuroscience show that machine learning can be usefully leveraged for scientific discovery and theory building.

By pairing cross-validated encoding/decoding frameworks with tools that can advance interpretability (e.g., featureimportance mapping, representational similarity analysis), affective neuroscientists have begun to translate distributed activation patterns into concrete hypotheses.

For example, the sharedrepresentations hypothesis proposes that witnessing another person's pain engages parts of the same circuitry as first-hand nociception, offering a compelling account of empathy (Preston & De Waal, 2002).
text.formatted: For example, the sharedrepresentations hypothesis proposes that witnessing another person's pain engages parts of the same circuitry as first-hand nociception, offering a compelling account of empathy <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">(Preston & De Waal, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Traditional brain-mapping studies, which consistently report partially overlapping activation in anterior insula and mid-cingulate cortex for both types of "pain," have been cited extensively as evidence for this view (Singer et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Traditional brain-mapping studies, which consistently report partially overlapping activation in anterior insula and mid-cingulate cortex for both types of "pain," have been cited extensively as evidence for this view <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">(Singer et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: However, multivariate predictive modeling reveals a more nuanced picture.

A neurologic pain signature (NPS) derived from first-hand pain does not generalize to empathic pain, while a distinct vicarious pain signature (VPS) predicts others' suffering yet remains insensitive to direct nociception (Kragel & Wager, 2019; Krishnan et al., 2016; Wager et al., 2013).

text.text: Importantly, the goal here was not to overturn the shared-representations hypothesis but to refine it; the functional dissociation of the two signatures sets a higher bar for future theoretical and computational models of empathy while preserving the empirical work that motivated the original account.
Not all computational affective neuroscience models are data-driven.
A growing body of work also seeks to integrate psychological theory and neurobiology through more structured frameworks.
For example, Bayesian models have been used to characterize how categoryspecific emotional brain responses vary across individuals and contexts (McVeigh et al., 2024; Wager et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For example, Bayesian models have been used to characterize how categoryspecific emotional brain responses vary across individuals and contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(McVeigh et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b170">Wager et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This is where computational affective science and neuroscience are poised to form a particularly virtuous cycle.

Mathematically explicit psychological theories can supply the priors that would guide neural modeling, while carefully crafted and validated neural models can return with posterior estimates and boundary conditions for further refinement of the same theories.

All in all, progress in formalizing broad theories of affect and motivation has been gradual, in part because different modeling frameworks use different feature sets and evaluation metrics, making apples-to-apples comparisons rare.
Framing computational models of emotional theories in a shared mathematical vocabulary would be a meaningful next step for computational affective science.

Theory-agnostic frameworks (e.g., Suri & Gross, 2022; Zhang et al., 2023) have begun to emerge, offering a provisional way of treating differing theoretical perspectives as special cases within a richer computational landscape.
text.formatted: Theory-agnostic frameworks (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b159">Suri & Gross, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref> have begun to emerge, offering a provisional way of treating differing theoretical perspectives as special cases within a richer computational landscape.

text.text: But the deepest synthesis that theory can offer is across levels: binding computational and algorithmic accounts of what emotion and motivation are to implementational accounts of how the brain makes them.

Realizing it will require more affective scientists fluent in formal modeling, and more modelers willing to engage deeply with emotion theory and neurobiology-the two-way fluency through which today's rich library of verbal theories might finally grow into an integrated science of affect and cognition.

From Charles Darwin sketching the facial expressions of emotion in humans and animals to William James meticulously cataloguing bodily feelings, affective science began as an observational enterprise.
Over the century and a half that followed, it matured into a rigorous discipline devoted to understanding the forces that energize and direct behavior.
The argument of this paper is that advances in understanding motivated behavior will require a shared formal language that integrates insights from affective and cognitive science.
As we saw from examples from meteorology and cognitive science, the scientific gains of such a shift are substantial.
Formal models can sharpen verbal theories, adjudicate among competing mechanisms, generate novel predictions, and build bridges across levels of analysis.

They also provide a shared language that can help dissolve the longstanding divide between affect and cognition, allowing researchers who study emotion, motivation, learning, memory, and decision-making to jointly contribute to a more integrated science of behavior.
But the case for embracing computational affective science goes far beyond the scientific arguments reviewed here.

So, before considering how the field might go about taking this next step, it is worth zooming out to consider what computational affective science could make possible for the world beyond the ivory tower.
Many of the gravest challenges of our time-intergroup conflict, political polarization, climate change-are, at their core, problems of human emotion and motivation.
We have long known that explanatory depth is the gateway to real-world impact (Aristotle, ca. 350 B.C.E/1984; Machamer et al., 2000).
text.formatted: We have long known that explanatory depth is the gateway to real-world impact <ref type="bibr">(Aristotle, ca. 350 B.C.E/1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Machamer et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Clearer causal models of affect can offer clearer understanding of why people act as they do and point to promising levers for designing more effective interventions.
The stakes are equally high for technology.
Today's artificial intelligence is extraordinarily capable, but only because we hand it its objectives; unlike humans and other animals, it has no intrinsic drive to explore and set goals of its own.
Building agents that do has been called the next frontier on the road to artificial general intelligence (Colas et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Building agents that do has been called the next frontier on the road to artificial general intelligence <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Colas et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A formal account of how motivated behavior emerges and becomes elaborated into the complex architecture of emotions, values, and goals is exactly what the extant work on motivated AI lacks, and exactly what computational affective science could supply, along with the ethical guardrails any artificial motivated system will need.
In each of these arenas, the road to deeper causal understanding runs through formalization.
Today, computational models are so commonplace in cognitive science that one can hardly open a journal without encountering one.
Other branches of psychology, including developmental (Shultz & Sirois, 2008), social (Cushman, 2024), and clinical (Montague et al., 2012), are increasingly following suit.

text.text: If the case for embracing computational affective science is so compelling, why has the field of affective science been slower to develop a cumulative computational tradition than its neighbors?
One common explanation is that affect is simply harder to formalize than cognition-that it is too subjective, too difficult to measure, too volatile (see Neisser, 1963; Simon, 1967).
text.formatted: One common explanation is that affect is simply harder to formalize than cognition-that it is too subjective, too difficult to measure, too volatile (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Neisser, 1963;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Simon, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: I do not believe this to be the case.
This intuition rests on the historical centrality of subjective experience in affective science.

But one does not need to look too far to see that the study of what has traditionally been relegated to the realms of cognition is no less reliant on measuring subjective experience than the study of motivation and emotion is.

Cognitive scientists routinely ask participants to reflect on their deeply held beliefs, rate subjective confidence in a decision, say whether a word feels familiar, and even describe their reasoning process out loud as it unfolds (Newell & Simon, 1961).
text.formatted: Cognitive scientists routinely ask participants to reflect on their deeply held beliefs, rate subjective confidence in a decision, say whether a word feels familiar, and even describe their reasoning process out loud as it unfolds <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Newell & Simon, 1961)</ref>.

text.text: These judgments have been the bedrock of formal theories for decades; and if such subjective data can support rigorous computational models of cognition, there is no principled reason why they cannot do the same for affective science.
Instead, the lag might be better understood as an artifact of how the two fields developed.
Affective science is comparatively young and unusually interdisciplinary, drawing on psychology, neuroscience, physiology, philosophy, anthropology, sociology, and clinical practice.
Although this breadth is indisputably a source of richness, it has also likely contributed to the field's fragmentation.
Much of modern affective science grew out of clinical psychology, where the immediate priorities were diagnosis and treatment rather than formal mechanistic explanation.
Several developments are now changing this picture.
Advances in artificial intelligence have made questions of motivation and emotion newly urgent well beyond psychology.

Within cognitive science, too, affect is moving from the margins of models toward their core, with models treating it as both emerging from the system's computations and shaping its subsequent behavior (e.g., Cervantes et al., 2017; Dubey et al., 2022; Eldar et al., 2016; Juvina et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Within cognitive science, too, affect is moving from the margins of models toward their core, with models treating it as both emerging from the system's computations and shaping its subsequent behavior (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Cervantes et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Dubey et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Eldar et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Juvina et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the evidence increasingly suggests that this move is not only elegant but necessary: building affect into cognitive models as a core component improves their predictions even in traditionally cognitive domains such as perception, learning, and memory (Stussi et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2016).

text.text: Taken together, these developments make this an especially opportune moment.

Amid what has been called the era of affectivism (Dukes et al., 2021), affective science now has both the rigorous foundations and the momentum it needs to take its own computational turn that will play a key role in shaping the next chapter in the science of the mind and behavior.

text.text: Where Do We Go From Here?
Across the areas reviewed in this paper, a common lesson emerges: translating hypotheses into computational terms accelerates both theoretical progress and practical application.
Models of specific phenomena sharpen theories; theories guide applications; and applications generate new phenomena that demand explanation.
Realizing the full potential of this virtuous cycle over the coming decade and beyond requires making progress on three fronts.
A basic fluency in formal and quantitative methods is broadly useful across the behavioral and cognitive sciences, which is why it is essential to cultivate it more deliberately.

Statistical and computational coursework in graduate education often lags behind the demands of contemporary research (Howard, 2024), and even graduate students trained within the same department may receive strikingly different methodological training depending on whether they are socialized into affective, cognitive, clinical, or neuroscience traditions.
text.formatted: Statistical and computational coursework in graduate education often lags behind the demands of contemporary research <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Howard, 2024)</ref>, and even graduate students trained within the same department may receive strikingly different methodological training depending on whether they are socialized into affective, cognitive, clinical, or neuroscience traditions.

text.text: Importantly, the goal is not for every affective scientist to become a mathematician.
Computational modeling is, first and foremost, a way of thinking, and adopting COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE that mindset can sharpen a verbal theory long before any code is written.

General literacy in computational modeling methods-enough to read a model critically, grasp what it does and does not commit to, and collaborate productively with computational modelers from cognitive science, computer science, engineering, neuroscience, and economics-is a much more productive and attainable target.
Above all, we need collaboration.
Global climate models were not built by the hand of a lone meteorologist.
Instead, the discipline leapt forward when physicists, mathematicians, and instrument-makers rallied around a shared problem.
Affective scientists, cognitive scientists, and modelers across disciplines can, and should, do the same.
Whether modeling the weather or the mind, once a computational model is specified, two questions emerge: how do we know if the model is any good, and what can we learn from it?

Philosophers of science have long noted that a model's clarity often comes at the steep cost of simplifications and idealizations, both of which are indispensable for understanding complex systems (Winsberg, 2010).
text.formatted: Philosophers of science have long noted that a model's clarity often comes at the steep cost of simplifications and idealizations, both of which are indispensable for understanding complex systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">(Winsberg, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The relevant question, therefore, is not whether a model is realistic in every respect, but whether it captures the features of a phenomenon that matter for making progress on the scientific question at hand.

In practice, a model earns credibility through a combination of theoretical coherence, empirical adequacy, and its ability to generate accurate out-of-sample predictions across contexts (Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017).
text.formatted: In practice, a model earns credibility through a combination of theoretical coherence, empirical adequacy, and its ability to generate accurate out-of-sample predictions across contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">(Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Meeting this standard as a field, rather than one lab at a time, will require shared infrastructure.

As things currently stand, models of the same phenomena are often tested on different tasks, measures, and populations, which makes it nearly impossible to tell whether two models disagree because their mechanisms differ or because their data do.

Adopting common, multimodal benchmark datasets and open modeling architectures would make head-to-head comparison of models from different traditions the norm rather than the exception (Carvalho & COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE Lampinen, 2026).
text.formatted: Adopting common, multimodal benchmark datasets and open modeling architectures would make head-to-head comparison of models from different traditions the norm rather than the exception <ref type="bibr">(Carvalho & COMPUTATIONAL AFFECTIVE SCIENCE Lampinen, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Investments of this kind have already paid off in computer vision, natural language processing, and climate science (e.g., Deng, 2009; Eyring et al., 2016).

text.text: Computational affective science must follow suit.
The final priority that I would like to emphasize is more careful description of the phenomena under study.
In Marr's (1982) framework, the computational level is itself a description, a precise statement of the problem a system solves.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Marr's (1982)</ref> framework, the computational level is itself a description, a precise statement of the problem a system solves.

text.text: A field becomes ripe for formal modeling only when its descriptive and theoretical foundations are sufficiently mature to support it.
Darwin did not develop a theory of evolution in a vacuum; he stood on the shoulders of naturalists like Linnaeus, whose painstaking descriptive work came first.
Computational affective science will require a similarly rigorous descriptive tradition.
Importantly, by "description" I do not only mean rich qualitative accounts.
Indeed, some of the most consequential descriptive work in cognitive science is rigorously quantitative.
For example, the classic finding that people are reliably faster to verify that "a canary has wings" than that "a canary has skin" (Collins & Quillian, 1969) is, at its core, descriptive in nature.
text.formatted: For example, the classic finding that people are reliably faster to verify that "a canary has wings" than that "a canary has skin" <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Collins & Quillian, 1969</ref>) is, at its core, descriptive in nature.

text.text: By describing regularities in response times, this work set the agenda for a generation of formal models of conceptual knowledge.
In affective science, analogous descriptive work is similarly essential.
Careful description also means attending to variability, because a model can only be as precise as the category it is trying to explain.

In closing, let us once again look to the sky for inspiration-only in this case, not just at the clouds above, but far, far beyond the Earth's atmosphere.
In the 20th century, astrophysicists used a model to predict the shape and timing of gravitational waves decades before they were ever observed.
Einstein hypothesized that events like collisions of two black holes should send ripples-known as gravitational waves-through the fabric of space (Einstein, 1916 (Einstein, /1996)).
text.formatted: Einstein hypothesized that events like collisions of two black holes should send ripples-known as gravitational waves-through the fabric of space <ref type="bibr">(Einstein, 1916</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Einstein, /1996))</ref>.

text.text: Following Einstein's prediction, physicists constructed a precise mathematical model of what those waves should look like if Einstein's theory were correct.

Their prediction became a reality in 2015, when LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) detected a signal that matched the predicted waveform almost perfectly (Caltech/MIT/LIGO Lab, 2016), confirming both the existence of gravitational waves and, importantly, lending support to the theoretical model that had anticipated them (Abbott et al., 2016).

text.text: Affective science is, of course, not astrophysics.
Its subject matter is closer to home, yet the broader lesson still holds.

Affective scientists, who have already spent decades building rich conceptual accounts of emotion, are in a position to begin a similar dialogue-aiming, in time, for quantitative forecasts and data capable of confirming or refuting those predictions with LIGO-level precision.
This effort will require more than any one discipline can provide.

It will require cognitive scientists who can specify mechanisms of learning, attention, memory, and decision-making; neuroscientists who can connect those mechanisms to biological implementation; computer scientists and engineers who can build and test artificial affective systems; clinicians who understand how affect breaks down; and affective scientists who can keep the field anchored in the phenomena that matter most.

Only by recognizing these efforts as part of the shared project of Computational Affective Science can we make their contributions add up to more than the sum of their parts: a truly cumulative science of behavior.

Are they devastated or overjoyed?
Answering requires combining what we see on their face with what we know about the situation and about the person.
